summary: An opinion column questioning why the Philippines passed a deficit national budget for 2024 when the Department of Budget and Management says a surplus budget policy encourages growth. It reports the House approval of the P5.768-trillion budget, explains budget concepts and deficit financing, and notes the projected P2.268-trillion deficit and rising debt. The author warns of inflation, political agendas, and the burden on future generations.
one_line: Opinion piece criticizes the Philippines' P5.768-trillion 2024 deficit budget, citing rising debt, inflation risks, and the DBM's own case for budget surpluses.
key_facts: The House of Representatives approved the P5.768-trillion 2024 national budget (House Bill No. 8980) on third and final reading on Sept. 27, 2023, by a vote of 296 to three with zero abstentions.
House Speaker Ferdinand Martin G. Romualdez said the budget process involved rigorous discussions, particularly on confidential and intelligence funds.

The DBM says a budget is balanced when revenues match expenditures; when expenditures exceed revenues the government incurs a deficit financed by borrowing, borrowing from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, or drawing down Treasury cash balances.
In 1994 the government broke the deficit trend by posting a budget surplus of P16 billion through privatization, revenue generation and prudent spending.
The DBM argues that less government borrowing reduces pressure on interest and inflation rates and leaves more funds for private businesses and families.
The 2024 budget of P5.768 trillion is 9.5% higher than the 2023 budget of P5.268 trillion, an increase of P499.6 billion, and equals 21.7% of GDP.
With about P3.5 trillion in tax revenues, the budget implies a deficit of some P2.268 trillion to be funded by additional borrowings.
Government debt could rise from P14.24 trillion (as of July) to P16+ trillion by the end of 2024.
Finance Secretary Benjamin Diokno projected tax revenue to rise from P3.5 trillion in 2023 to P6.5 trillion in 2028, while non-tax revenues decline from P191 billion to P184 billion.
Diokno said the Finance department aims to reduce net financing from P1.42 trillion in 2022 to P1.22 trillion in 2024, bringing debt-to-GDP almost below 60% by 2025.
President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. said the Philippines' debt-to-GDP ratio stands at about 63%, which is 'a little high for us and it is not ideal.'
Assistant National Statistician Rachel Lacsa said the country needs a 3.7% average inflation rate over the next five months to hit the BSP's 5.5% forecast for 2023.
The author, Amelia H. C. Ylagan, a doctor of Business Administration from the University of the Philippines, asks how many generations will pay for the debt.
